value.label: No IPv6 broadcast

value.label: IPv6 vs IPv4
value.description: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and a different packet/header model; IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses and its own packet format.

value.label: Unicast vs anycast vs multicast
value.description: IPv6 defines all three transmission/addressing modes with different destination semantics.

value.label: Multicast vs broadcast
value.description: IPv6 has no broadcast; all-nodes multicast supplies the analogous attached-link all-host function.

value.label: SLAAC vs DHCPv6
value.description: SLAAC is stateless host/router-based prefix configuration; DHCPv6 can supply additional stateful addresses or information.

value.label: Link-local vs global unicast
value.description: Link-local addresses are local-link and required on IPv6 interfaces; global unicast addresses are globally routable.

value.label: Base header vs extension headers
value.description: The base header is fixed at 40 octets; optional functions are moved to extension headers.

value.label: Router fragmentation vs endpoint fragmentation
value.description: IPv6 routers do not fragment; endpoints can fragment and hosts can use PMTU discovery.

value.label: IPv6 no header checksum vs IPv4 checksum
value.description: IPv6 omits the base-header checksum, unlike IPv4, reducing router recalculation work.

value.label: Dual-stack vs tunneling
value.description: Dual-stack runs both stacks natively; tunneling encapsulates one protocol within another network.

value.label: IPv4-mapped vs IPv4-compatible
value.description: IPv4-mapped addresses remain a hybrid representation; IPv4-compatible addresses are deprecated.

value.label: Stable vs temporary addresses
value.description: Stable/global identifiers support reachability but can facilitate tracking; temporary addresses reduce persistence.

value.label: AAAA vs A DNS records
value.description: AAAA resolves IPv6; A resolves IPv4.

value.label: PMTU discovery vs fragmentation
value.description: PMTU discovery sizes packets for the path; fragmentation is endpoint-only when needed.

value.label: IPsec vs higher-layer security
value.description: The source discusses IPsec at the IP layer but does not equate it with TLS; both occupy different architectural positions.

value.label: Native vs tunneled IPv6
value.description: Native IPv6 traverses IPv6-capable infrastructure; tunneling carries IPv6 over IPv4 infrastructure.

value.title: IPv6 is just IPv4 with bigger addresses
value.correction: IPv6 changes packet format, address architecture, fragmentation behavior, neighbor discovery, multicast/broadcast semantics and other protocol functions.

value.title: IPv6 supports broadcast
value.correction: IPv6 does not define traditional broadcast addresses; multicast is used instead.

value.title: Routers fragment IPv6 packets
value.correction: IPv6 routers do not fragment; hosts use PMTU discovery or endpoint fragmentation.

value.title: IPv6 addresses always need DHCP
value.correction: IPv6 supports SLAAC and hosts generate link-local addresses automatically; DHCPv6 is optional for additional state.

value.title: Every IPv6 address is globally routable
value.correction: IPv6 interfaces require link-local addressing and may have multiple address types; global unicast is only one category.

value.title: IPv6 cannot be scanned
value.correction: The source explicitly notes that configuration patterns can make scanning feasible in real-world scenarios.

value.title: IPv6 has a header checksum like IPv4
value.correction: IPv6 omits the base-header checksum.

value.title: IPv6 and IPv4 interoperate directly
value.correction: The source states the protocols are not directly interoperable and require transition mechanisms.

value.title: IPv6 extension headers are always harmless to routers
value.correction: Some implementations process extension headers in software/CPU paths, causing performance or security issues.

value.title: Global IPv6 addressing eliminates privacy concerns
value.correction: Stable globally addressable identifiers can facilitate tracking; temporary addresses mitigate this concern.

value.title: Tunneling is equivalent to native IPv6
value.correction: Tunneling adds encapsulation and can reduce MTU/increase latency.

value.title: NDP is just ARP with a new address format
value.correction: NDP uses ICMPv6 and multicast and also handles router discovery and address configuration.

value.title: AAAA records are IPv4 DNS records
value.correction: AAAA records map names to IPv6 addresses; A records map names to IPv4.

value.title: IPv6 deployment means IPv4 disappears immediately
value.correction: The source describes coexistence and transition mechanisms because both protocols operate simultaneously.

value.title: IPv6 security is automatically stronger because of the larger address space
value.correction: The source identifies implementation and operational security risks, including shadow networks and fragmentation evasion.

source_claims.title: IPv6 purpose and origin
source_claims.claim: IPv6 was developed to address anticipated IPv4 address exhaustion and provide a successor IP protocol.

source_claims.title: 128-bit addressing
source_claims.claim: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and an address space of 2^128.

source_claims.title: Address architecture
source_claims.claim: IPv6 uses hierarchical addressing, generally with a 64-bit routing prefix and 64-bit interface identifier.

source_claims.title: Transmission modes
source_claims.claim: IPv6 supports unicast, anycast and multicast and omits broadcast.

source_claims.title: Autoconfiguration
source_claims.claim: IPv6 hosts create link-local addresses and can configure global addresses using router advertisements and SLAAC.

source_claims.title: Neighbor discovery
source_claims.claim: NDP replaces the IPv4 ARP role using ICMPv6 and multicast.

source_claims.title: Packet structure
source_claims.claim: IPv6 packets have a 40-octet base header plus optional extension headers and payload.

source_claims.title: Router fragmentation
source_claims.claim: IPv6 routers do not fragment; hosts use PMTU discovery or endpoint fragmentation.

source_claims.title: DNS integration
source_claims.claim: AAAA records provide IPv6 DNS resolution and ip6.arpa supports reverse resolution.

source_claims.title: Transition
source_claims.claim: Dual-stack and tunneling allow IPv4/IPv6 coexistence; NAT64 provides translation mechanisms.

source_claims.title: Security
source_claims.claim: IPv6 security includes IPsec support but also shadow-network and fragmentation-evasion risks.

source_claims.title: Standardization
source_claims.claim: IPv6 evolved from IPng through RFC 1883, RFC 2460 and RFC 8200.

source_claims.title: Deployment
source_claims.claim: IPv6 deployment has expanded through ISPs, operating systems, mobile networks and Internet services, with the source citing 2026 adoption measurements.

value.name: Runtime execution pipeline
value.expression: source → JavaScript engine → execution frames/call stack → event loop/message processing → host APIs/I/O
value.mechanism: The engine executes JavaScript inside a host runtime; the runtime supplies APIs and schedules messages.

value.name: Event-loop processing
value.expression: message_queue → event_loop → call_stack_frame → run_to_completion → next_message
value.mechanism: Messages are processed one at a time; each message runs to completion before the next is considered.

value.name: Dynamic value typing
value.expression: variable → value(type A) → reassignment → value(type B)
value.mechanism: Type is associated with the value rather than the variable/expression.

value.name: Operator-dependent coercion
value.expression: operands + operator → coercion rules → result
value.mechanism: Binary + may concatenate after string coercion, while - converts operands to numbers.

value.name: Prototype delegation
value.expression: object.property → own property? → prototype chain lookup → inherited method/property
value.mechanism: Property lookup walks prototype relationships when a property is not directly owned.

value.name: Lexical closure
value.expression: outer lexical environment + nested function → retained internal state
value.mechanism: A nested function retains access to outer bindings after the outer function finishes.

value.name: Promise/async model
value.expression: async operation → Promise → handlers / await → eventual result
value.mechanism: Promises represent eventual results; async/await structures non-blocking asynchronous code.

value.name: Browser security boundary
value.expression: Web script → sandbox + same-origin policy + CSP → constrained execution
value.mechanism: Browser restrictions limit system capabilities and cross-origin data access, while CSP constrains trusted executable content.

value.name: XSS attack chain
value.expression: attacker-controlled input → malicious script in target page → victim privileges → data/action compromise
value.mechanism: The malicious script executes in the target application's security context.

value.name: CSRF attack chain
value.expression: attacker page → victim browser → authenticated target request → unintended state change
value.mechanism: Cookie-based authentication can cause cross-site requests to carry valid credentials.

value.name: ECMAScript standardization evolution
value.expression: Netscape JavaScript → Ecma submission → ECMAScript editions → annual proposal process
value.mechanism: Standardization moved from browser-specific implementations toward a shared evolving language specification.

value.name: JavaScript/WebAssembly execution complement
value.expression: JavaScript → performance-critical region → WebAssembly → same engine sandbox
value.mechanism: WebAssembly complements JavaScript for performance-critical portions while remaining inside the engine's sandbox.

value.distinction: JavaScript is the language/ecosystem as used in practice; ECMAScript is the standardized language specification.
Despite name/syntax similarities, JavaScript is dynamically typed and prototype-based while Java is statically typed and class-based.
ECMAScript defines language semantics but not I/O; a runtime supplies networking, storage, graphics, and host APIs.
Dynamic typing concerns when/how types are associated with values; weak typing concerns implicit coercion across operations.
JavaScript's underlying inheritance remains prototype-based even when class/extends/super syntax is used.
The source states there is no distinct definition form; invocation context determines whether a function acts as a method via this.
The source describes JavaScript execution as single-threaded with queued messages and non-blocking I/O.
Promise is an asynchronous result abstraction; async/await is syntax for structuring asynchronous operations.
Sandbox limits system capabilities; same-origin policy limits cross-origin information access.
XSS executes attacker-controlled script in a target page; CSRF induces a victim browser to send an unintended authenticated request.
Client-side validation improves user experience but cannot be the sole security enforcement point.
Obfuscation can hinder inspection but does not make client-side code or embedded secrets confidential.
The source lists both but does not define a strict semantic boundary between them.
TypeScript is presented as a statically typed/strict language that transpiles to JavaScript.
WebAssembly complements JavaScript for performance-critical portions and runs in the same sandbox.
Vanilla JS means standard JavaScript without third-party libraries/frameworks.
Both use JavaScript engines, but their host runtimes expose different environment APIs.
The source contrasts Java's compiled-bytecode loading with JavaScript being loaded as human-readable source code.
var is function-scoped; let and const are block-scoped.
const prevents reassignment of the binding; the source does not state that referenced objects become deeply immutable.

value.misconception: JavaScript is Java.
value.correction: They are distinct languages with substantially different typing, object models, loading models, and histories.

value.misconception: ECMAScript and JavaScript are completely separate languages.
value.correction: JavaScript conforms to the ECMAScript standard; ECMAScript specifies the core language while hosts provide APIs.

value.misconception: Dynamic typing means JavaScript has no types.
value.correction: Types exist on values; variables can be rebound to values of different types.

value.misconception: Weak typing means JavaScript is dynamically typed.
value.correction: Dynamic typing and weak typing describe different properties: value-associated typing versus implicit coercion.

value.misconception: JavaScript inheritance is class-based underneath.
value.correction: The source states class syntax abstracts an underlying prototype inheritance mechanism.

value.misconception: const makes an object immutable.
value.correction: The source states const prevents reassignment of the binding; it does not define deep object immutability.

value.misconception: Client-side JavaScript can securely enforce validation.
value.correction: Client validation is convenience; security enforcement must also occur on the server.

value.misconception: Obfuscating JavaScript hides secrets.
value.correction: Client source can be extracted and obfuscation can be reverse-engineered.

value.misconception: CSP alone fixes all JavaScript security problems.
value.correction: CSP is one control; XSS, CSRF, dependency, browser, and sandbox issues remain distinct.

value.misconception: XSS and CSRF are the same attack.
value.correction: XSS executes malicious script in a target context; CSRF abuses a victim browser to make an unintended authenticated request.

value.misconception: JavaScript is single-threaded, therefore it cannot perform concurrent I/O.
value.correction: The event-loop model permits non-blocking I/O while messages are processed sequentially.

value.misconception: Web APIs are part of ECMAScript itself.
value.correction: The source explicitly separates ECMAScript language facilities from host-provided I/O and Web APIs.

value.misconception: WebAssembly replaces JavaScript.
value.correction: The source presents WebAssembly as complementary, especially for performance-critical portions.

value.misconception: Vanilla JS is a separate programming language.
value.correction: It is a term for using standard JavaScript without libraries/frameworks.

value.misconception: JavaScript only runs in browsers.
value.correction: It runs in Node.js, Deno, Bun, application frameworks, JVM contexts, and some embedded systems.

value.misconception: A function and a method are different language constructs in JavaScript.
value.correction: The source says the distinction occurs during invocation; method calls bind this to the receiver.

value.misconception: All JavaScript engines interpret source without compilation.
value.correction: Modern engines commonly use JIT compilation to improve performance.

value.misconception: Prototype pollution is ordinary prototype inheritance.
value.correction: Prototype pollution is a runtime vulnerability involving attacker modification of prototype properties.

value.misconception: Third-party package dependencies are automatically trustworthy.
value.correction: The source highlights stale, vulnerable, malicious, or removed dependencies as a supply-chain risk.

value.misconception: Browser sandbox bugs are only theoretical.
value.correction: The source cites historical cases where incorrect privilege handling enabled vulnerabilities.

JavaScript dominates client-side Web scripting and is widely used through libraries/frameworks.
JavaScript is dynamically and weakly typed, prototype-based, multi-paradigm, and supports first-class functions and closures.
Browser sandboxing and same-origin policy constrain JavaScript, while XSS, CSRF, prototype pollution, dependency risks, and browser flaws are security concerns.
JavaScript extends beyond browsers through Node.js, Electron, Cordova, React Native, Acrobat, GNOME Shell, and embedded systems.
Browser developer tools, linters, profilers, and benchmark tools support JavaScript development.
JavaScript influenced and was influenced by other languages/technologies and is complemented by JSON, transpilers, and WebAssembly.

value: Kubernetes primarily represents desired state as objects; controllers determine corrective actions rather than requiring users to script every individual machine operation.

spec expresses desired state; status records current state.

Service provides stable identity/load balancing over a changing set of Pods.

Container filesystems can disappear on restart; volumes provide persistent/shared storage.
CRD defines an API type; Operator combines custom resources with controllers to automate domain-specific behavior.
Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides what that identity may do.
kubelet manages Pod state; runtime executes container lifecycle through CRI.

CSI separates storage integration implementation from Kubernetes core.
Scheduler decides where an unscheduled Pod runs; controllers continuously reconcile resource state.

value.misconception: Kubernetes is a virtual machine hypervisor
value.correction: Kubernetes orchestrates workloads; it can run on virtual machines or bare metal but is not itself the VM hypervisor.

value.misconception: A Pod is just a container
value.correction: A Pod is the deployable unit and can contain one or more co-located containers.

value.misconception: A Service is a Pod with a stable IP
value.correction: A Service is an abstraction over a selected set of Pods and provides stable network identity.

value.misconception: Scheduler keeps desired replica counts
value.correction: Scheduler places unscheduled Pods; controllers reconcile resource state and replica counts.

value.misconception: etcd runs containers
value.correction: etcd stores cluster state; container runtime executes containers on nodes.

value.misconception: Secrets are automatically encrypted at rest
value.correction: The source explicitly notes Secrets are not encrypted at rest by default and require additional setup.

value.misconception: Namespace alone provides full security isolation
value.correction: Namespaces partition resources, while authorization controls API permissions.

value.misconception: StatefulSet itself is a database
value.correction: StatefulSet provides identity/order orchestration properties; the database remains the application.

value.misconception: kubelet decides cluster-wide placement
value.correction: kubelet maintains workload state on its node; scheduler selects nodes.

value.misconception: Reconciliation is a one-time deployment step

value.correction: Pods can be replaced; Services provide stable IP/DNS identity.

source_claims.title: Definition
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized workloads.

source_claims.title: Cluster model
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes assembles virtual or bare-metal computers into a cluster capable of running container workloads.

source_claims.title: Control-plane/node architecture
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes separates management/control-plane components from worker nodes and exposes resources through an object/API model.

source_claims.title: etcd state store
source_claims.claim: etcd persistently represents cluster configuration/state and favors consistency during network partitions.

source_claims.title: API server
source_claims.claim: The API server exposes the Kubernetes API, validates REST requests, persists API-object state, and participates in watch-driven coordination.

source_claims.title: Scheduler
source_claims.claim: The scheduler matches unscheduled Pods to nodes using resource availability and constraints.

source_claims.title: Controllers
source_claims.claim: Controllers reconcile actual cluster state toward desired state and can replace failed workloads.

source_claims.title: kubelet
source_claims.claim: kubelet maintains Pod/container state on each node and reports node status.

source_claims.title: Runtime_CRi
source_claims.claim: The container runtime manages container lifecycle while CRI decouples kubelet from implementation.

source_claims.title: Networking
source_claims.claim: kube-proxy implements network proxy/load-balancing behavior for Services.

source_claims.title: Namespaces
source_claims.claim: Namespaces segregate Kubernetes resources across teams/projects/environments.

source_claims.title: Pods
source_claims.claim: Pods are the basic deployable unit and group one or more co-located containers with a Pod network identity.

source_claims.title: Workloads
source_claims.claim: Higher-level workload objects declaratively manage Pods, including ReplicaSets, Deployments, StatefulSets and DaemonSets.

source_claims.title: Services
source_claims.claim: Services provide stable IP/DNS identity and load-balance traffic to Pods selected by labels.

source_claims.title: Storage
source_claims.claim: Volumes, persistent storage, Container Attached Storage, and CSI address storage persistence and external storage integration.

source_claims.title: Configuration
source_claims.claim: ConfigMaps and Secrets externalize configuration; Secrets are intended for confidential data and require additional protection for at-rest encryption.

source_claims.title: API objects
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes objects record intent with metadata, spec, status, ownership, and lifecycle semantics.

source_claims.title: Extensions
source_claims.claim: CRDs, custom controllers, and Operators extend Kubernetes declaratively.

source_claims.title: API security
source_claims.claim: TLS, authentication, and authorization mechanisms protect the Kubernetes API.

source_claims.title: Cluster API
source_claims.claim: Cluster API applies Kubernetes object/API principles to infrastructure and machines.

source_claims.title: Uses
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes is used across deployment, scaling, cloud/data-center management, observability, and related infrastructure workflows.

source_claims.title: Complexity/criticism
source_claims.claim: The source discusses complexity, ecosystem fragmentation, operational difficulty, and reasons managed services/PaaS approaches emerged.

source_claims.title: History
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes originated at Google, drew on Borg and Promise Theory, was announced in 2014, and was contributed to CNCF.

source_claims.title: Release timeline
source_claims.claim: The source contains a release/support timeline through Kubernetes 1.36 and related support windows.
